doc.title: Vincent Pelote interviewed by Monk Rowe, Orlando, Florida, February 25, 2017

title: Interesting people met: Leonard Feather, Gunther Schuller and Benny Carter
summary: Pelote did research for Feather, met Schuller, and asked Benny Carter a naive question about when tuba and banjo gave way to bass and guitar.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: Who are the most, I don’t know, short list of the most interesting people you’ve met doing your work?

Well I didn’t meet him, but I did some work for him, long distance work for him. I did some work on Leonard Feather’s book, Earwitness to an Era.” I think it was his last book. And he couldn’t come out to the Institute so he sort of hired me to do some digging and stuff. And he paid me nicely, gave me check and everything. And I knew of him, I

knew about him from reading and all of that and I knew all of the great things he did in terms of promoting the music and everything. And so I was very happy and proud to work for Leonard Feather. As far as meeting other people, Gunther Schuller, I met Gunther Schuller who I thought was one of the nicest people ever. He was doing some work on his book about the Swing Era. He pulled out about a ton of LPs and sat down and listened to these things over and over and over again, which was great. And I really enjoyed him. And believe it or not I met him at the Institute, Bennett Lester Carter. Benny Carter. He came over, well, the Ed Berger connection. Ed’s father wrote the definitive biography of Benny Carter, and Ed wrote the discography. It was a two-volume thing. The first volume was the history of Benny, the biography. The discography was the second volume. And Ed did that whole thing. And it was wonderful. It was the second, I thought, comprehensive discography of an artist at that time, the first being Hendersonia, Walter C. Allen’s book, which is huge. But it’s a biodiscography of Fletcher Henderson that Walter C. Allen must have worked on forever. But it came out first, and then Benny’s book came out with Ed’s discography, which is just as comprehensive as anything Walter Allen did, maybe even more so in some ways. So when Benny came to the Institute, I even remember the first stupid question I asked him, I wish I could have taken that back, I said, “Well Benny,” you know, trying to show I know a little something about jazz, I think I might have called him Mr. Carter even, I wasn’t that comfortable with him yet. And I said you know, “Mr. Carter, could you sit down and tell me when the switchover from tuba and banjo, the switchover to bass and guitar. When did that happen exactly.” Like there was an exact date that this happened, some magical date. And he looked at me like I had three heads. But he was such a nice guy. He didn’t say what a stupid question. He just said, “Well,” he said, “some arrangements called for tuba and banjo and some arrangements called for bass and guitar.” And that pretty much was it.
There was no magical moment when this happened.
It just sort of evolved in time. And yeah I guess he was right.

I know. It’s like you want those things to have this — like when did music switch back to straight eighth notes. Well the day Chuck Berry — I mean you want this thing to be compartmentalized a little bit.
